t: Coastal states often remove new settlements by force soon after they appear
body: When people build or settle within reach of an existing country, that country has often sent police, marines or troops within weeks or months. In 1964 a Dutch company called REM built a steel platform in the North Sea, about 10 kilometres off Noordwijk, to broadcast advertising-funded television. The Netherlands passed a law in December 1964 that reached the platform through the seabed it stood on, and on 17 December boats and police helicopters arrived. Accounts differ on whether marines or police officers boarded. In Italy, the engineer Giorgio Rosa declared his platform off Rimini, Rose Island, independent on 1 May 1968. Police and tax officers took control of it about eight weeks later, and the government ordered it demolished.

The Minerva Reefs, between Fiji and Tonga, followed a similar course. In 1972 the Nevada property developer Michael Oliver backed a republic on sand piled onto the reefs. Australia, New Zealand, Fiji and other neighbours supported a Tongan claim, Tonga annexed the reefs in June, meaning it formally added them to its territory, and on 21 June its king sailed out with soldiers and the platform was dismantled within hours. When a group of Americans went back in 1982, Tongan troops forced them off after three weeks. In the Caribbean, gunboats ordered Werner Stiefel's Operation Atlantis off the Silver Shoals reef.

The same thing has happened in recent years. An American bitcoin trader, Chad Elwartowski, and his Thai partner lived in a small floating cabin about 14 nautical miles off Phuket until the Thai navy raided it in April 2019. They had already left, and Thailand charged them under a law that carries life in prison or death. How the case ended is not known. On the Danube, Croatia has detained visitors to Liberland, a self-declared state on land between Croatia and Serbia, since 2015. Police arrested its founder, Vit Jedlicka, in September 2023 after supporters built wooden shelters, and the camp was removed that month. The founder of Verdis, a similar claim nearby, says Croatian authorities destroyed his group's camp within days that October.

An unarmed group has no way to stop a patrol boat or a police unit, so a settlement within reach of a state lasts only as long as that state allows it. In most of these cases the removal came before any court had ruled on the legal argument. Someone planning a settlement near a coast therefore needs a plan for what happens when officials arrive, in addition to a legal theory about where the border runs.

t: Governments have changed the law after people used a legal boundary
body: Several projects were placed just past a legal boundary, usually the edge of the territorial sea, the belt of coastal water a state fully controls. At the time Britain and the United States set that belt at three miles. In 1964 Radio Caroline began broadcasting pop music to Britain from a ship outside British waters, where it needed no British licence. Britain could not reach the ship, so a law of 1967 made it a crime for anyone under British law to supply it or advertise on it. Off Los Angeles, gambling ships anchored past the three-mile limit from 1928 because California banned gambling on land. California raided them in 1939, and a federal ban followed in 1948.

Courts also moved the line by measuring it differently. Roy Bates, a former British army major, was convicted over a radio station on the Knock John sea fort, and his appeal failed in 1967. The court held that the fort lay inside the limit, because distance is measured from a line fixed by law that need not follow the shore. In the Radio 390 case, the High Court counted the limit from a sandbank visible only at low tide. Bates moved to Roughs Tower, farther out, and declared it the Principality of Sealand. In 1987 Britain extended its territorial sea to 12 miles, which took in the tower. Britain has not removed the occupants, and one caretaker still lives on the fort.

States have also reached projects through the seabed. The Dutch law that ended REM Island reached the platform through the sea floor it stood on, although accounts differ on whether it declared that seabed Dutch territory or applied Dutch law to installations on the Dutch part of the continental shelf. In United States v. Ray in 1970, an American appeals court stopped two rival plans for new countries on reefs off Florida, because the reefs were part of the continental shelf, the shallow seabed off a coast where a state has exclusive rights to resources. The United States used the same reasoning against a later plan for a nation on Cortes Bank, off San Diego.

A project placed outside a legal boundary depends on that boundary staying where it is, and governments can move it by passing a law or winning a court case. They can also act indirectly by making rules for the project's suppliers, customers and citizens, or by claiming the seabed it stands on. Sealand is the one lasting case, and it has lasted because Britain has not acted against it since the limit changed.

t: Selling passports, bonds or land for a country that does not exist
body: Some projects have earned money by selling documents, shares or land titles for a country that was never built. The oldest large case is Poyais. In the 1820s the Scottish adventurer Gregor MacGregor sold bonds and land in an invented nation on the Caribbean coast of what is now Honduras, and about 250 settlers sailed there and found only jungle. At least 180 of them died. New Utopia, promoted from the mid-1990s, offered bonds in a tax-free country to be built on concrete platforms in the Caribbean. The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which polices investment sales, sued its promoter in 1999. The SEC says about $24,000 was raised, while encyclopedia entries claim $100 million.

Other schemes were larger or lasted longer. The Dominion of Melchizedek, declared in 1990 by the American Mark Pedley, claimed reefs and islands it did not hold and sold passports and bank licences. One of its investment schemes took more than $4 million from at least 1,400 people. The Kingdom of EnenKio, which claimed Wake Island in the Pacific, marketed $1 billion in bonds online until an American court froze its promoter's assets in 2000. Later projects used digital tokens. Satoshi Island sold tokens for a planned city on a leased island in Vanuatu, and in 2025 its company said they could no longer be traded because of a breach of the land lease.

Some of these sales are closer to novelties, and buyers may understand that. Dennis Hope filed a claim to the Moon in 1980 and has sold deeds full time through his Lunar Embassy since 1995. Discover magazine reported more than $9 million in sales at $19.99 a sale. Legal experts say the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, blocks such private claims, and no government has ruled on the deeds. Asgardia, a self-declared space nation, took online sign-ups and reported about 290,000 registered citizens in 2019, and no state recognises it. Some sales were ordinary business failures. Life at Sea Cruises sold 111 cabins for a three-year voyage, called it off in November 2023, and after weeks of silence admitted that it had no ship.

A passport, bond or land deed from an unrecognised country gives its buyer only what the seller chooses to deliver, because no state or court is bound to honour it. Ordinary law still applies to the seller. American regulators have acted against bond sales aimed at American investors whatever territory the offer claimed. Anyone raising money for a new country from the public therefore comes under the investment and fraud laws of the places where the buyers live.

t: Most attempts issue their own money, and it rarely works outside the group
body: A currency is one of the first things many new countries announce, because it is cheap to make. Sealand, the former sea fort off Britain, has issued coins since 1972, nominally equal to the US dollar. Minerva had coins that included a 35-dollar piece. Operation Atlantis struck a silver coin called the deca on a soap press. New Atlantis, a raft off Jamaica, named a currency called the scruple, made up of items such as fish hooks and shark teeth. Molossia, a joke country on private land in Nevada, uses paper circles on poker chips and sets them at 80 American cents. Recent projects use digital tokens, such as Liberland's Merit and the Solar planned by Asgardia.

Such money can be used among members and sold to collectors, but it has little use beyond that. International payments pass between banks that hold accounts with each other, called correspondent banks, and a place with no banking law or supervisor gives them no one to rely on. Banks also book payments using standard currency codes, and without one a currency has no standard listing on normal payment systems. A token sold to outsiders comes under the crypto and money-transfer rules of the buyers' countries, such as the European Union's crypto regulation and the American stablecoin law of 2025.

Having a real government does not solve the problem. Transnistria, a breakaway territory in Moldova with its own army and central bank, issues a ruble that can be exchanged only inside the territory. Inside a recognised country, the state can also stop private money altogether. Martin Coles Harman, who owned the English island of Lundy, issued his own coins in 1929, and a court convicted him under the Coinage Act of 1870 because the island was part of England.

Issuing an internal currency is one of the easiest steps for a new project, and it shows little about whether the project will work. Residents still need dollars, euros or bitcoin to pay for imported food, fuel and equipment, and they need a bank or an exchange willing to handle those payments.

t: Storms, engineering failures and lack of money have ended many attempts
body: Many projects at sea ended before any government had to respond. In 1966 a group planning a country called Abalonia on Cortes Bank, off San Diego, towed an old concrete freighter out to serve as its base, and waves broke it apart on the rock. Tropical storms destroyed Leicester Hemingway's raft republic off Jamaica. Werner Stiefel's Operation Atlantis lost a boat to a storm in the Bahamas and an oil rig to a hurricane. In February 2024 a wave broke in two the barge on which the Italian businessman Samuele Landi lived off Dubai, and he and two employees died.

Other ships failed on insurance and cost. The company Ocean Builders bought the cruise ship MS Satoshi in 2020 to anchor it off Panama as a floating community. No insurer would give it liability cover, so it could not keep a crew, a safety rating or a flag, and the company sold it within weeks. Freedom Ship, a floating city proposed in the late 1990s, has gone from an estimated $6 billion in 1999 to as much as $20 billion in 2026, and nothing has been built. The residential ship Villa Vie Odyssey did sail, from 2024. On 26 October 2026 more than 200 residents were told to leave the ship in Cambodia because the company could not secure fuel.

Projects in space have mostly ended the same way. Mars One, a Dutch venture that planned a one-way colony, was declared bankrupt by a court in Basel in January 2019 with debts of about 1 million euros. Orion Span's Aurora Station, a proposed orbital hotel, closed without starting construction. Bigelow Aerospace, which did fly inflatable modules, laid off all 88 staff in March 2020. The two best-known asteroid mining firms, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, were both sold by January 2019 without mining anything.

The places where law leaves the most room, such as the open ocean and outer space, are also the most expensive and dangerous places to live. A project in those places has to pay for shelter, supplies, insurance and rescue with no nearby state to provide them. Its budget and engineering therefore often decide its future before any legal question comes up.

t: Living beyond land borders usually depends on registering with an existing state
body: The ships and space stations where people have lived long term all keep an existing state in the arrangement. At sea this state is the flag state, the country where a ship is registered and whose law applies on board. MS The World, a ship of 165 homes owned by the people who live on it, has been registered in the Bahamas since it was completed in 2002. Women on Waves, a Dutch group that takes women to international waters to give them abortion pills, sails a Dutch-registered ship under Dutch law. When two Portuguese warships blocked it in 2004, the European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2009 that Portugal had breached freedom of expression.

Space works in a similar way. Under the 1998 treaty on the International Space Station, each partner keeps legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens on board. Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty requires a country to authorise and supervise its companies in space, so planned private stations such as Vast's Haven-1 stay under American supervision. Asgardia, a self-declared space nation, launched one small satellite in 2017 on a US mission, and it stayed under American authority.

Flying a flag with no state behind it gives no protection. In 1946 a British destroyer stopped the Asya on the high seas after she hauled down a Turkish flag and raised a Zionist one. In 1948 the Privy Council, then the final court for the British Empire, held that freedom of the open sea belongs to ships that fly and are entitled to fly the flag of a state. In United States v. Marino-Garcia in 1982, an American appeals court upheld the drug convictions of foreign crewmen on a stateless vessel, with nothing linking the cargo to the United States. That ruling binds courts in one part of the United States, and no international court has endorsed it.

Licensing also gives states control over hardware they cannot physically reach. The American company Swarm launched four small satellites on an Indian rocket in 2018 after the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) refused it a licence. The FCC still had power over it, because Swarm was an American company and its satellites sent signals to ground stations in the US state of Georgia. It paid a $900,000 penalty. Sea Launch fired rockets from the open Pacific until 2014, from a rig on Liberia's register, through a company registered in the Cayman Islands, and one legal article says this made it hard to say which state was the launching state. American export rules still applied, because they follow the company and its technology. In 1998 the State Department suspended the project's export licences for about two months over 207 violations, and Boeing, its manager, paid $10 million. Lawyers have asked whether spacecraft could use flags of convenience, registering in a country with light rules as merchant ships do, but the launching country stays liable for damage and no court has tested the practice.

A person can live away from any one country's daily control by living on a registered ship, as residents of The World do. This requires accepting the law of the flag state, along with permission from each port and the rules of insurers. It provides private ownership and rules agreed among residents, and it provides no independent legal territory. Anyone who wants more than that has no working example to follow at sea or in orbit.

t: Claims with nobody on the land can last for decades because no government needs to act
body: Many of the longest-running claims involve no one living on the land. A self-declared state of this kind is often called a micronation. Westarctica has claimed Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica since 2001, when an American navy intelligence specialist read that no country had claimed it. He wrote to many governments, and only other micronations replied. Flandrensis, begun by a Belgian in 2008 as a two-week hobby, claims five islands off West Antarctica and now runs as a Belgian non-profit about melting ice. Neither can gain legal ownership, because the Antarctic Treaty bars new claims.

Other claims concern land no one wants or can reach. In 2014 the Virginia farmer Jeremiah Heaton planted a flag at Bir Tawil, a stretch of desert that neither Egypt nor Sudan claims, and declared a kingdom so that his daughter could be a princess. He applied for observer status at the United Nations, and other people later declared their own states on the same land. No government has recognised any of them, and in international law only states can take land that belongs to no state. In 1949 James Mangan, a public relations man from the Chicago area, registered a claim to all of outer space with a county office in Illinois. No government is reported to have acted on it.

Many micronations inside existing countries are art, protest, tourism promotion or a hobby. Key West, Florida, declared itself the Conch Republic in 1982 to protest a federal roadblock, and the name now serves as tourism promotion. Molossia, a joke country on private land in Nevada, pays property tax to its county, so the county has no dispute with it. A claim runs into trouble when its owner acts on it. Edwin Lipburger, who declared his spherical house in Austria a republic, was sentenced to 10 weeks in prison in 1979 for acting as a public official without the right to do so.

The long life of these claims says nothing about their legal strength. They continue because they cost no government any money or attention. A claim that starts to affect taxes, borders, investors or criminal law usually draws a response from the state concerned, as the other patterns show.

t: A government can grant a zone its own rules, and a later government can take them back
body: The most practical way to get separate courts or tax rules today is to ask an existing government to grant them. The Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) is a 110-hectare business district created by Dubai's own laws in 2004. Its courts, working since 2006, hear civil and commercial cases in English under common law, the English system built on past court rulings. Criminal and immigration law still apply there, and the zone remains part of Dubai.

Honduras shows how such a grant can end. In 2013 it changed its constitution to allow zones with their own laws, courts and taxes, and Próspera was built under this law on the island of Roatán with American venture capital. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal in 2022, and the Supreme Court declared the zone laws unconstitutional in September 2024. Próspera's owners had claimed about $10.8 billion from Honduras at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, a World Bank body that decides disputes between investors and governments. Honduran officials said in 2025 that the claim had dropped to $1.63 billion. The case was still pending in October 2026, and the zone continues to operate.

Smaller promises have ended in the same way. French Polynesia signed a memorandum with the Seasteading Institute in 2017 for a floating settlement in a lagoon, and after local objections the government said in 2018 that the document had no legal force. Senegal's state tourism agency said in 2025 that Akon City, the singer's planned city, no longer existed and that a more realistic project had been agreed in its place. Malaysia's local council revoked the business licence of the Network School in July 2026, and within hours Kazakhstan's digital ministry signed a memorandum to host a campus. The oldest examples have stronger foundations. Vatican City rests on a 1929 treaty with Italy, and the monks of Mount Athos govern themselves under Greek law.

Two long-running arrangements show the same limit. Florida created the Reedy Creek district around Walt Disney World in 1967, with votes going by land, one per acre, so Disney in effect chose the board. After Disney opposed a state education law in 2022, the legislature voted to dissolve such districts, and in February 2023 the state kept the district under a new name and gave the governor the appointment of its board. In the Bahamas, an agreement of 1955 let the Grand Bahama Port Authority build and administer Freeport. A tribunal in a partial award reported in March 2026 rejected the authority's argument that it had exclusive authority, and it confirmed that the government keeps its regulatory authority there.

A zone of this kind can give its founders working courts and tax rules, and it rests on the host country's law. Elections, court rulings and local opposition can all change that law. A treaty with the host, as the Vatican has, has given more protection than a memorandum or a licence. An investment treaty may allow a company to claim money after a repeal, without restoring the zone.

t: Places that run as states mostly began with war or long self-rule, and recognition stays a political choice
body: Recognition means that other states formally accept a place as a state. The governments that have won any of it did not begin with a declaration on empty ground. Somaliland, in the Horn of Africa, emerged from a 10-year war and has run its own elections, government and currency since 1991. Israel became the first UN member to recognise it on 26 December 2025, and it remained the only one in October 2026. Taiwan has about 23.3 million people and its own elections, and it has formal relations with 11 UN members and the Holy See, because China refuses relations with any country that recognises it.

A supporting state with an army often decides whether such a place survives. Russian troops helped Transnistria in 1992 and remain there. Northern Cyprus was formed after Turkey invaded in 1974, and only Turkey recognises it, in part because UN Security Council Resolution 541 urged members to refuse. Abkhazia and South Ossetia, on land Georgia claims, are recognised by Russia and three other UN members. Wa State in Myanmar has its own army and runs its own affairs under a 1989 ceasefire, and it accepts Myanmar's sovereignty over its territory. Force can also end these governments. Azerbaijan took the rest of Artsakh in September 2023, and almost its entire population left. Syria's government launched an offensive against the Kurdish-led administration in the north-east in January 2026, and by August its bodies had merged into the Syrian state.

The Order of Malta is the one case with no land. This Catholic religious order lost its last territory to Napoleon's forces in 1798, and other countries went on treating it as a sovereign body. Its website reports diplomatic relations with 118 countries, while Wikipedia gives 115 states. Its standing comes from centuries of history that a new group does not have.

Other states decide on recognition according to their own interests, and meeting the usual tests of population, territory and government does not guarantee it. No project on the open sea, on Antarctic ice or in space has been recognised by a UN member. A new group with no population or armed protector has no clear way to obtain it.

t: States are setting the rules for space, the seabed and Antarctica
body: Treaties bar anyone from owning the Moon, the deep seabed or new parts of Antarctica, but states still act in these places in ways that shape what comes next. In 1976 eight equatorial countries claimed the part of geostationary orbit above them, the ring where a satellite stays over one spot. Other countries rejected the claim. Tonga applied for orbital slots from 1990 and rented them to satellite operators. In 2007 a Russian expedition planted a titanium flag on the seabed at the North Pole, and other governments said it had no legal effect. Chile and Argentina placed families and schools in Antarctica, including the birth of Emilio Palma at an Argentine base in 1978, although Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty says such acts cannot support a claim.

Resources are now the main subject. A US law of 2015 lets American citizens own materials they mine in space while disclaiming any national ownership of the body they came from. Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates and Japan have passed similar laws, and no court has tested them. The Artemis Accords, a non-binding set of principles drawn up by the United States, reached 78 signatories in October 2026. They allow safety zones around activities on the Moon, and China and Russia are planning a separate lunar base with their own partners. The 1979 Moon Agreement, which calls the Moon's resources the common heritage of humanity, has 17 members and no leading space power among them.

The deep seabed shows the same contest. The International Seabed Authority, set up under the 1982 Law of the Sea treaty, controls mining outside any country's waters, and it has not finished its mining rules. In April 2025 President Trump ordered the American ocean agency NOAA to speed up permits under an older American seabed mining law, and within days The Metals Company's American arm applied, outside that system. NOAA found in April 2026 that the application met the law's information requirements, and it took public comments until 19 October 2026. The authority opened an inquiry into the company's two subsidiaries, which hold contracts under the treaty, and on 18 July 2026 a specialist chamber of the law of the sea tribunal ordered it to respect fair procedure, with the main case undecided. No American permit had been issued by August 2026.

The treaties that bar ownership in these places bind only their members and leave many questions open, and state practice is filling in the answers. Private founders have had little part in this. A private project in one of these places would depend on the rules and licences of whichever state or group of states it works with.

t: Land left outside borders by accident stayed free only while its neighbours allowed it
body: Places outside any state's control have existed, usually because of a mistake or a disagreement between neighbours. Cospaia, in central Italy, came about in 1440 because a treaty set a border at a creek called the Rio and two creeks had that name. The land between them belonged to neither side for nearly four centuries, until Tuscany and the Papal States divided it in 1826. Neutral Moresnet, between what are now Belgium and Germany, was created in 1816 because the Netherlands and Prussia could not agree who should have a zinc mine. Germany annexed it during the First World War, and the Treaty of Versailles gave it to Belgium. Couto Misto, three villages on the border of Spain and Portugal, ran its own affairs for centuries until a treaty of 1864 divided it.

Others lasted a shorter time. About 17,000 people in Germany ran the Free State of Bottleneck from 1919 to 1920, after Allied occupation zones left their area cut off. Settlers on the strip now called the Oklahoma panhandle, which belonged to no state or territory, set up a government called Cimarron Territory and asked Congress to recognise it in 1887. Congress did not, and the strip joined Oklahoma Territory in 1890. Kowloon Walled City in Hong Kong grew to about 33,000 people because neither Britain nor China would enforce its authority there. Once the two governments had agreed on Hong Kong's future, they announced its demolition in 1987.

International rulings set out how land with no owner can be acquired, and they speak of states. Terra nullius is the legal term for land that belongs to no state. In the Island of Palmas case of 1928, the arbitrator held that continuous and peaceful government of a place gives a stronger title than discovering it or being close to it. In the Clipperton case of 1931, France kept an empty Pacific island on the strength of a formal claim, public notice and a brief landing in 1858.

Each of these places lasted because the states around it found it easier to leave things as they were, and each ended when those states agreed or one of them acted. Land that is left out today, such as Bir Tawil and Gornja Siga, exists for the same kind of reason. It may also be disputed. The founder of Enclava, in 2015, read online that a plot between Slovenia and Croatia was unclaimed, and Slovenia then said it was part of a claim before an international court, which gave the parcel to Slovenia in 2017. A private person gets no title from occupying such land, because the law treats it as open only to states.

t: How new states have been created on land where a people already lives
body: New countries still appear, and they form when a people already living on a territory separates from a state. South Sudan voted 98.83% for separation in January 2011, in a referendum fixed by a 2005 peace agreement with the government in Khartoum, and joined the UN that July. Eritrea's rebels won a long war against Ethiopia in 1991, and 99.83% voted for independence in a UN-observed vote in 1993. Montenegro used an exit clause in its union with Serbia and won 55.5% in 2006, and outside powers accepted the result within days. Timor-Leste became independent in 2002 after Indonesia agreed to a UN-run vote that followed 24 years of occupation.

A vote does not always lead to independence. Wikipedia's table lists about 123 independence referendums since 1817. Counting its outcomes gives 59 ending in a No, 31 in a Yes followed by independence and recognition, 16 in a Yes with no independence, and 12 in a Yes with control on the ground and no general recognition. Western Australia voted Yes in 1933 and stayed in Australia. Catalonia voted in 2017 against an order of Spain's Constitutional Court. No state recognised its declaration, and Spain took direct control of some regional powers. Bougainville voted about 98% for independence in 2019 and is still waiting for a decision by Papua New Guinea's parliament, which has the final say under the peace agreement.

Recognition by outsiders has limits too. Biafra was recognised by five states and ended when it lost a civil war against Nigeria in 1970. Kosovo declared independence in 2008, and the International Court of Justice said in 2010 that this did not break international law. It is recognised by 110 UN members, but it has not joined the UN. In the other direction, South Africa declared four homelands for its black population independent between 1976 and 1981 to serve its apartheid policy, and apart from South Africa and the four themselves, which recognised one another, no government accepted them.

Success has usually required an existing population with a history on the land, along with the agreement of the old state, a military victory or both. A group of investors or settlers without those things cannot use this route, however detailed its constitution. For a people who do have them, the terms agreed with the state being left have mattered a great deal in whether other countries accept the result.

t: States sell territory to other states, and buying land from a state gives only ownership
body: Countries have sold land to each other for centuries, transferring sovereignty, the legal right to rule a place. The United States paid France $15 million for Louisiana in 1803, Russia $7.2 million for Alaska in 1867 and Denmark $25 million for the Danish West Indies in 1916. Pakistan bought Gwadar from Muscat and Oman in 1958, and the last sale on Wikipedia's list came in 1963, when West Germany paid the Netherlands 280 million Deutsche Marks for Elten, Selfkant and Suderwick. Every buyer and seller on that list is a state or a ruler. Even an agreed transfer can stall. Egypt's president ratified a treaty in June 2017 giving Tiran and Sanafir to Saudi Arabia, the handover was still unresolved in 2023, and sources differ on where it stands now. A sale needs a willing seller. Denmark refused an American offer of $100 million in gold for Greenland in 1946, and Danish and Greenlandic leaders have refused again since 2019.

Modern founders have looked for a government willing to sell, and none has agreed. Michael Oliver tried to buy an island from a government before his group piled sand on the Minerva Reefs in 1971. Werner Stiefel tried to buy the Prickly Pear Cays near Anguilla for $100,000, and the sale fell through. Anton Bakov, a Russian businessman, reported failed talks with Kiribati and the Gambia as of 2017. Theodor Herzl, a founder of Zionism, offered the Ottoman sultan money and later debt relief for rights in Palestine in 1896 and 1901, and the sultan refused. Dryden Brown of the company Praxis said he flew to Greenland in 2024 to try to buy it, and a Danish MP replied that independence needs the Danish parliament's approval.

What a buyer can get is ordinary ownership under the seller's law. Kiribati, itself a state, paid $8.6 million in 2014 for an estate in Fiji, and it holds that land as an ordinary owner under Fijian law. Larry Ellison owns 98 per cent of the Hawaiian island of Lānaʻi, which is still part of a US county and state. The Robinson family can keep visitors off Niʻihau, and the island is still under United States rule. The Fullard-Leo family won private title to Palmyra Atoll against the federal government in 1947, and the atoll stayed under United States sovereignty throughout. The farmer Leonard Casley owned the land of his self-declared Hutt River and was still ordered to pay tax.

Buying land gets a person a title deed and leaves the existing state's tax, criminal and planning law in place, however complete the ownership is. A transfer of the right to govern needs a treaty or an act by the government giving it up. Since no modern government has offered this to a private buyer, a purchase on its own does not create a new country. The older private deals that did give ruling powers form a separate pattern.

t: Private buyers who gained ruling rights over territory, mostly before 1900
body: Private people did once obtain the right to rule territory, and in three cases this led to a recognised state. Liechtenstein began as a purchase. A rich noble family bought Schellenberg in 1699 and Vaduz in 1712 from an indebted count, with the emperor's approval, because it needed land to win a seat in the Imperial Diet, the assembly of the Holy Roman Empire. The emperor joined the two into a principality in 1719, and it became sovereign in 1806 when Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine took it out of the empire. King Leopold II of Belgium held the Congo Free State as his personal possession from 1885 until Belgium annexed it in 1908. His agents gathered treaties with local leaders, and he gained the state through recognition by the United States and the European powers at the Berlin Conference. His rule brought forced labour, torture and murder, and poor records leave the number of deaths uncertain. Liberia began when a private American society acquired land from a local ruler in 1821, perhaps under threat of force. The settlers themselves declared independence in 1847.

Many others ruled under a higher power, which kept sovereignty or took it back. The Sultan of Brunei's representative granted James Brooke the area around the town of Sarawak in 1841 in return for military help, with no sale price, and the sultan confirmed the appointment by July 1842. The family ruled as rajahs until one of them ceded Sarawak to Britain in 1946, over the objection of his heir. The British North Borneo Company bought rights from two sultans in 1877 and 1878 and governed under a British charter until 1946. The Hudson's Bay Company held Rupert's Land around Hudson Bay under a royal charter from 1670 and sold it through the Crown to Canada for £300,000 in 1869. The Rudd Concession of 1888 gave Cecil Rhodes's agents mineral rights only, and it was used to win a charter under which a company took and governed what is now Zimbabwe. The Knights of Malta bought four Caribbean islands from a failing French company in 1651 and the governor Jacques du Parquet bought others in 1650. The French king stayed sovereign in both cases. The Knights sold theirs on in 1665, and the king cancelled the company's private sales in 1664. In the Cocos Islands, the Clunies-Ross family received the land in 1886 while Britain kept sovereignty. The lordship of Sark could be bought only with the monarch's consent, as it was in 1852, and in 1765 a noble family sold its rights over the Isle of Man to the British Crown for £70,000.

Other purchases gave no ruling rights, or the rights were cancelled. In the United States, the Supreme Court ruled in Johnson v. M'Intosh in 1823 that private citizens could not buy land from Native American nations, because only the sovereign could acquire it. Virginia and North Carolina threw out Richard Henderson's Transylvania purchase from the Cherokee, and the Governor of New South Wales declared John Batman's 1835 deed with Aboriginal elders void. New Zealand's 1840 Treaty of Waitangi made the Crown the only lawful buyer of Māori land, which put the New Zealand Company's deeds under review. Merchants' deals sometimes led to colonies when their governments stepped in, as with Adolf Lüderitz in what is now Namibia and the Rubattino Company at Assab in Eritrea. Several of these deals rested on terms the seller did not understand or later rejected.

Nearly all of these grants date from before 1900, when an emperor, king or sultan could hand over land and ruling rights by a personal act and outside powers decided what to accept. The last of them, the Bolivian Syndicate's 1901 lease over Acre, was bought out in 1903, and the Sarawak and North Borneo cessions of 1946 ended the two longest-running private governments in Borneo. No private purchase made in the 20th or 21st century is known to have produced sovereignty. A buyer today would need a government willing to give up territory by treaty, and none has been reported doing so for a private party. Old contracts can still lead to money claims. Heirs of the Sultan of Sulu won a $14.92 billion award against Malaysia in 2022 over the 1878 Borneo deal, and Malaysia announced in December 2025 that a Paris court had annulled it.

t: Large land purchases and leases since 1990 have not transferred sovereignty
body: Foreign companies and rich individuals have made very large land deals in recent decades, and critics often call them land grabs. In 2008 the South Korean company Daewoo Logistics agreed a 99-year lease on 1.3 million hectares of farmland in Madagascar to grow corn and palm oil for export. Anger over the deal helped drive President Marc Ravalomanana from office in March 2009, and his successor said it was off because the constitution barred selling or renting out land. In what is now South Sudan, the Texas company Nile Trading signed a 49-year lease over about 600,000 hectares for $25,000 in 2008. Local chiefs and officials took their objections to the president in 2011, and the deal is reported as stalled. The American financier Philippe Heilberg of Jarch Capital bought rights to 400,000 hectares through a warlord's son, saying he was betting that African states would break apart. Whether those rights were ever enforced is not known.

Some deals were limited or cancelled by governments. In 2011 Iceland's interior minister refused the Chinese businessman Huang Nubo an exemption from a law barring large land purchases by buyers from outside Europe's single market. In 2019 a provincial government in the Solomon Islands gave a Chinese developer exclusive development rights over the island of Tulagi, and the national Attorney-General declared the agreement unlawful within weeks. Others went ahead. In 2024 a state investment fund from the United Arab Emirates agreed to pay Egypt for rights to develop Ras El-Hekma on the Mediterranean coast, in a $35 billion agreement, and Egypt kept a 35 per cent stake. In Albania, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump plan a resort on the island of Sazan and the coast opposite it, after a 2024 law opened the protected area to five-star hotels. Environmental groups have gone to court, and thousands protested in Tirana in June 2026.

Private owners can hold huge areas under another country's law. Douglas Tompkins, founder of The North Face, bought more than a million hectares in Chile and Argentina for nature reserves. Chile's parliament debated whether his land, running from the Pacific to the Argentine border, undermined national sovereignty. The Benetton clothing group holds about 970,000 hectares in Argentine Patagonia, under a title that goes back to an 1889 state grant made without the consent of the Mapuche people, and an Argentine civil court has ruled for the company against Mapuche occupants, with the result of the appeal not known. A lease can also give a company wide practical control. Kings Romans, a Hong Kong-registered company, runs a casino zone on a 99-year lease in Laos where the clocks are set to Beijing time and the usual currency is the yuan, and the land is still Laos. An older example is Firestone, whose 1926 lease and loan gave it a say over Liberia's state finances while Liberia stayed independent.

In all of these deals the land remained under the state that granted it, and each investor's position depended on that state's law and politics. Governments have cancelled or blocked deals after changes of leader, protests or legal reviews. Local and Indigenous residents are often left out of the terms and have challenged them. A buyer can gain control over use of the land and in some cases great influence, and none of these deals gave a buyer the legal right to govern.

t: Attempts to take over existing governments with hired soldiers
body: A few people tried to take over an existing country with mercenaries, soldiers for hire, in place of founding a new one. In November 1981 Mike Hoare, a veteran of mercenary wars in the Congo, led 53 men against the government of Seychelles with encouragement from apartheid South Africa. Nine went ahead, and the other 44 arrived at the airport disguised as rugby players and members of a beer-drinking charity club, where a security officer found a rifle in one man's bag. After a gunfight most of them hijacked an airliner to South Africa.

Other plots were stopped before they reached their targets. In April 1981 American agents arrested white supremacists at a marina in New Orleans as they prepared to sail to overthrow the government of Dominica, after a boat captain they approached reported them. In March 2004 police in Zimbabwe impounded a Boeing 727 carrying 64 former soldiers bound for Equatorial Guinea, and arrested the former British officer Simon Mann by the runway. He was later sentenced to more than 34 years in Equatorial Guinea and pardoned in 2009. Mark Thatcher, son of the former British prime minister, was fined in South Africa for his part.

Bob Denard, a French mercenary, came closest to lasting success. In May 1978 he overthrew the leader of the Comoros, an island country in the Indian Ocean, with 43 men and the backing of Rhodesia's government. He then ran the presidential guard for 11 years. He left in 1989 after the president was shot and after talks with French representatives. When he landed again in 1995 with about 30 men, the French army ended the attempt within about a week.

These plots need weapons, transport and money that pass through other countries, and most were stopped at those points, before any serious fighting. The only long success depended on the tolerance of France, the strongest outside power in the region. People who take part also face prosecution afterwards in the countries they pass through or attack, as several of these plotters did.

t: People can live for years in places between authorities without governing them
body: Some people have lived in places where normal government is limited. Mehran Karimi Nasseri, an Iranian man without papers, lived in Terminal 1 of Charles de Gaulle Airport near Paris from 1988 to 2006. Edward Snowden spent 39 days in a Moscow airport's transit area in 2013 until Russia granted him asylum. Julian Assange, the co-founder of WikiLeaks, stayed nearly seven years in Ecuador's embassy in London, because British police may not enter an embassy without its government's permission. In April 2019 Ecuador ended his asylum and invited the police in.

Others live in zones emptied by war or disaster. About 14,000 people live in four villages inside the UN-patrolled buffer zone across Cyprus, by listed populations for 2021. Two villages remain inside the demilitarised zone between North and South Korea, and residents of the southern one keep South Korean citizenship and must spend most nights there. People known as self-settlers went back to the Chernobyl exclusion zone without approval, and their numbers fell from 314 in a 2007 census to about 25 by April 2026. In California, up to 4,000 people spend the winter at Slab City, a camp on a former Marine base with no local government, where state and federal law apply and are largely not enforced.

None of these people held the land or made law for it. French law applied in the airport throughout Nasseri's stay, and Ecuador alone decided how long Assange could remain. Peacekeepers or armistice bodies set the rules in the buffer zones, and no declaration of a separate state in them is known.

A place like this can shelter a person for years. It gives that person no power to make laws, admit other people or deal with foreign governments, and those are the powers a founder of a new country wants. The arrangement also lasts only as long as the authorities responsible allow it or choose not to enforce the rules.

t: New islands, underground spaces and high platforms have stayed under existing law
body: Founders have sometimes hoped that a new kind of place would fall outside existing rules, but new land has been claimed quickly. Graham Island rose from the sea south of Sicily in July 1831. A Sicilian customs official planted an oar on it to claim it for the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and a British naval captain claimed it in August. It had worn away by December. In 1963 three French journalists jokingly claimed Surtsey, a new volcanic island off Iceland, and Iceland said at once that it was Icelandic and later made it a nature reserve. New land usually rises close to a coast or onto an island a state already holds, as at Nishinoshima in Japan. Such islands can also vanish. The island formed at Hunga Tonga in 2015 was mostly destroyed by an eruption in 2022.

Going underground does not change a place's legal position. Land ownership reaches downward only as far as the law of the country allows. Under the Law of the Sea treaty, a coastal state controls the rock under its continental shelf, including by tunnel. CyberBunker, a web-hosting business in a former NATO bunker in the Netherlands, called itself an independent republic. It later bought a second bunker in Germany, which 600 police raided in September 2019. A court in Trier convicted all eight defendants in 2021 of belonging to a criminal organisation, and Germany's Federal Court of Justice largely upheld the verdict in 2023. Other deep sites, such as the Pionen data centre under Stockholm and the shelters sold by Vivos, operate as ordinary property under national law.

Ice and the upper air offer little more. Writers disagree about the legal status of a free-floating iceberg, but icebergs do not last. A23a, for years the world's largest, was about 3,500 square kilometres in January 2025 and was thought to be gone or nearly gone by July 2026. Stratobus, a French robotic airship designed to hover 20 kilometres up, carries no people, with none planned, and needs certification and flight authorisation. Sky Cruise, a flying hotel, exists only as an animated video.

So far no new place has given anyone more than a short or legally uncertain period outside a state's law. People using these places have also depended on a country for supplies, licences and land access. A founder considering one of them has to expect that the law of the nearest or registering state will apply.

t: Indigenous and older peoples have gained self-rule mainly through courts and negotiation
body: The largest gains in self-rule have gone to peoples with a claim older than the state that now rules them. The Inuit negotiated a land claim with Canada, and Nunavut, a territory of 2,093,190 square kilometres, began in 1999 with a mostly Inuit population. In McGirt v. Oklahoma in 2020, the US Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 that Congress had never ended the Muscogee (Creek) reservation, and a state court applied the same reasoning to nine other nations, so most of eastern Oklahoma counts as Indian country for prosecuting serious crimes by Native Americans. Later rulings narrowed the effect. Sámi people elect their own parliaments in Norway, Sweden and Finland, and none of these parliaments claims independence.

Some communities took self-rule first and won legal backing or tolerance later. Cherán, a Purépecha town in Mexico, drove out illegal loggers, police and politicians in 2011, and Mexico's federal Electoral Tribunal backed its request to choose leaders by custom. The Zapatistas, a mainly Mayan movement in Chiapas, have run their own communities since their armed rising in 1994. The Mohawk community of Ganienkeh in New York occupied a former camp in 1974 and moved under a negotiated lease in 1977, and courts have since ruled against its land trust over back taxes.

Full separation has stayed out of reach. The Haudenosaunee, or Iroquois, have issued passports since at least 1923. Japan, Israel and Ireland have accepted them on some occasions, and Britain refused them for a lacrosse team in 2010. The Murrawarri in Australia declared a republic in 2013 after the Crown did not answer a demand to show any treaty, and the Australian government has not acknowledged it. Russell Means's Republic of Lakotah declared a withdrawal from treaties in 2007 without the backing of Lakota tribal governments, and it made no progress. Native Hawaiian groups remain divided on what they want after a US apology in 1993 for the overthrow of the kingdom. The Central Tibetan Administration, based in India, runs elections for Tibetans abroad with no land, and no country recognises it as a government.

Outsiders have tried to borrow this standing, and courts have limited what it covers. Tribes in the United States are immune from suits by private parties. In 2014, in a case over the Bay Mills Indian Community's casino at Vanderbilt, Michigan, the Supreme Court held that the immunity reaches business off the reservation and said that limiting it is the job of Congress. It also said that a state can act against the responsible individuals. In 2018 a federal appeals court refused to let the drug maker Allergan protect its patents from a government review by transferring them to the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe, because a tribe is not immune from action by the federal government. In 2019 another appeals court held two online lenders of the Lac Vieux Desert Band to be arms of the tribe, and in 2025 the same court upheld a judgment of $43,401,817.47 against the outside investor, Matt Martorello. International forums have not filled the gap either. In Larsen v. Hawaiian Kingdom in 2001, an arbitration panel said it could not decide whether Hawaii is part of the United States, because the United States was not a party.

Where these claims have succeeded, the people involved had a real population and history on the land, and they won their gains through negotiation or courts of the state they live in. The result has been greater self-rule inside that state. A new group of founders has no comparable claim, so this route is not open to it.

t: States reach people in open places through nationality, licences, parts, ports, banks and insurers
body: No state owns the high seas or outer space, so no government can treat them as its territory. People who go there still stay within reach of governments, because a state can apply its law to a person, a company or a ship that has some tie to it. The state acts at the point where that tie shows, which is often a court, a port or a bank on land.

The first tie is nationality. Italy's Council of State, the country's top administrative court, rejected the sovereignty claims for Rose Island by reasoning from its builder's citizenship, since an Italian who builds and profits from a platform outside territorial waters stays under Italian law. Britain could not reach Radio Caroline's ship, so its 1967 law made it a crime for anyone under British law to supply the ship or advertise on it. Off Phuket in 2019, one occupant of a floating home was a Thai citizen and the other held a Thai visa, which gave Thailand direct power over them whatever the status of the water. Giving up a nationality does not end a former state's claims for tax it says is owed. Roger Ver renounced his American citizenship in 2014 and was arrested in Spain in 2024 on an American tax indictment, and in 2025 he agreed to pay $49.9 million. A bought passport can also be weak abroad. In the Nottebohm case of 1955, the International Court of Justice held that Liechtenstein could not claim on behalf of a man who had no genuine connection with it when it made him a national.

The second tie is the licence. The American company Swarm launched four satellites on an Indian rocket in 2018 after the US Federal Communications Commission refused it a licence. The agency reached it because it was an American company and its satellites sent signals to ground stations in Georgia, and it paid $900,000. The same agency fined Dish Network $150,000 in 2023 for leaving a satellite too low in its disposal orbit, about 36,000 kilometres up, in a part of space no country may claim.

Parts and supplies give a third tie. American export rules treat rocket technology as defence technology and follow the company and the goods, wherever the launch takes place. Sea Launch fired from the open Pacific from a rig on Liberia's register, and in 1998 the State Department suspended its licences over 207 violations, and Boeing, its manager, paid $10 million. Camp Barneo, a Russian camp on drifting Arctic ice, relied on flights from Norway's Svalbard, and Norway imposed a flight ban in 2016. A court in Los Angeles held in 1939 that it had power over the operators of gambling ships past the three-mile line and over their water taxi owners, because they had been served with papers inside California.

Ports and air routes work in a similar way. Women on Waves could give abortion pills under Dutch law at sea, but two Portuguese warships kept its ship from reaching port in 2004, and the European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2009 that lighter steps would have been enough. The submersible Titan had no flag or certificate and worked beyond Canada's 200-mile zone. After it imploded in 2023, Canada's safety board aimed its recommendations at the Canadian-flagged support ship, because that is where a state can reach. In the air, an English court held that the Republic of Cyprus could refuse scheduled flights to Northern Cyprus, an area it does not control.

Banks and insurers are private, and they often act before any government does. MS Satoshi was to anchor off Panama in 2020, and no liability insurer would cover it. Without insurance there could be no crew, and without a crew it would lose its safety rating and its flag. In Somaliland, money-transfer firms such as Dahabshiil serve as the financial system, and in 2013 Barclays decided to close such firms' accounts after a record American fine against HSBC. A British court delayed the closure without cancelling it. When a government does act, payment links give it a route. Liberty Reserve, a private digital currency in Costa Rica, was shut in 2013 by American prosecutors working with authorities in 17 countries, and its founder received 20 years. Code can be harder to reach than people. An American appeals court held in 2024 that Tornado Cash's unchangeable software was not property that could be sanctioned, while its developers were still prosecuted in two countries.

A ship that loses its flag loses its own state's objection. Cameroon expelled the tanker Smyrtos from its register in May 2026, Britain boarded her the next month, and her captain was charged under British sanctions law, with trial set for 15 December 2026. Accounts differ on whether the boarding took place on the high seas or in British waters. Acting without any state's authority also carries risk. In 2013 an American appeals court held that Sea Shepherd's attacks on whalers in the Southern Ocean could count as piracy, and in 2015 the group agreed to pay $2.55 million for contempt over attacks by its foreign affiliates.

None of these steps gives a state title to the sea or to orbit, and the treaties that bar such claims remain in place. Courts have set some limits, and how far a state may go against foreigners on a ship with no flag is still argued. A project in an open place would meet these links at each point where it touches land, money or a licensed service.

t: Questions the law has not settled, and who argues what
body: On many of the rules for places outside every country, no court has given an answer. The treaties are silent or unclear on these points, and governments and legal writers take different sides. What follows sets out the main questions still open and who says what.

The first is what a state may do to a ship with no nationality. Article 110 of the Law of the Sea treaty lets a warship board and examine such a ship, and it does not mention prosecution. Writers divide. The "any state" view holds that any country may apply its law to a stateless vessel, and the American ruling in Marino-Garcia in 1982 took that line. The "nexus" view requires some link, such as the crew's nationality. In 2025 Andrew Norris argued that states may assert full jurisdiction, and in 2026 Thea Coventry of Leiden argued that boarding does not by itself give power over foreigners' conduct. In June 2025 a group of Nordic and Baltic states said vessels without a valid flag have no right to freedom of navigation. No international court has decided the point.

The second is who may take resources from places no one owns. The United States never joined the seabed part of the treaty system, and The Metals Company has applied for a permit under American law while its subsidiaries hold contracts under the treaty. The United States told the International Seabed Authority in July 2026, by the company's account, that it is not bound by those mining rules and does not regard them as customary law. Whether one country's permit can give a right to mine an area most of the world has agreed to manage together is unresolved. In space, an American law of 2015 lets citizens own what they extract while disclaiming ownership of the body. Critics argue that it breaches Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, which bars national appropriation. A supporter writing at Opinio Juris says Congress avoided the conflict, and Luxembourg's own Council of State said it was unclear whether international law allows such a law. No court has tested any of these laws.

Safety zones on the Moon raise a related question. Signatories of the Artemis Accords say the zones coordinate work and still respect free access by others. Critics fear that a zone others must keep clear of could work in practice like a claim. Russia called the Accords an attempt to create space law that favours the United States, and Chinese government-affiliated media compared them to colonial land-taking. No court has tested them.

The third is how far the space treaties reach. A treaty binds its members, and a rule can also become custom, which binds everyone. Whether that has happened to Articles I, II, VI and VII of the Outer Space Treaty is a live question. A writer in Völkerrechtsblog calls Articles II and III customary and cites Hobe and others as treating the ban on appropriation as a rule no state can opt out of. No court has ruled. The words "territory or facility" in the launching-state definition also remain undefined. Marco Pedrazzi writes that a ship or aircraft could be considered a facility of the state of registration, which gives no answer for a platform with no flag. Adrian Taghdiri warned that some countries would set loose rules to attract space companies, and no court has tested flags of convenience in space. Article 3 of the 1961 statelessness treaty covers births on ships and aircraft, and it does not mention spacecraft, so its reach to a birth in orbit would have to be argued by analogy.

Boundaries and categories are open too. No treaty says where airspace ends and outer space begins. Legal writers describe a spatial camp, which wants a fixed height, and a functional camp, which would classify an object by what it does. Denmark uses 100 kilometres for its own licensing law and told the UN that this does not prejudge its view of international law. The Law of the Sea treaty does not define "artificial island", or say whether a small floating home on a mooring is an island, an installation or a ship. No treaty names the owner of a floating iceberg. The writer Mateusz Osiecki concluded that it is probably no state's property, and he cited a study setting out three views, that it belongs to no one, that it can be property under a national claim, or that it is common property.

Statehood itself is under discussion. In 2025 the International Court of Justice said the loss of one element of a state "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood". Judge Tomka called this a precocious leap of legal reasoning and wrote that territory has been indispensable to the concept of a state, while Vice-President Sebutinde and Judge Aurescu wanted it firmer. All 193 UN members agreed in September 2026 to presume that a state continues despite sea-level rise. Where a submerged state's population would live and where its government would sit remain open, and none of this creates new states. Svalbard shows an older dispute over treaty rights. Norway reads the equal rights in the 1920 treaty as covering only the islands and their territorial waters, and Russia says they also cover Norway's 200-mile fishery zone.

Private arrangements have open questions of their own. Próspera's tribunal has not ruled on whether promises made under a law later declared void can support a claim. Erick Brimen points to Article 96 of the Honduran constitution, which says a law has no retroactive effect except in some criminal cases, and the lawyer Juan Carlos Barrientos answers that the article concerns penalties and that the constitutional chamber may apply its rulings to the past. Whether courts elsewhere will respect the shield of a nearly anonymous Marshall Islands company for token holders has not been decided, and a California court held in 2024, at an early stage of the Lido case, that a group of token holders can be pleaded as a general partnership, a ruling that did not concern a Marshall Islands registration. According to a report by a Mexican attorney, a local court enforced an award that used the blockchain jury system Kleros, and a later commentator stressed that the court enforced the human arbitrator's award. Pure on-chain rulings remain untested.
Any of these points could be settled by a court ruling, a new treaty or the steady practice of states. Until that happens, each position described here is an argument made by the people named.
